pairs.rationale: Both urge submission to governing authorities for a God-oriented reason. Peter names king and governors and says submission is for the Lord's sake; Romans explicitly grounds the existing authorities in God's appointment.

The stated conclusion about resisting God's ordering follows the preceding premise that existing authorities have been appointed by God. This is the letter's own premise-and-consequence argument, rather than an independent narrative about a particular ruler.
Both describe the public authority's contrasting response to evil and good: punishment of evildoers and praise of those doing good. Romans develops that contrast through the question about fear.

The earlier prohibition reserves repayment to the Lord; this verse describes an authority as God's avenger for wrath. The comparison follows vengeance and wrath language while distinguishing private retaliation from the described public role.

Romans adds conscience to the motive of avoiding wrath. Peter describes enduring unjust sorrows out of awareness of God. The shared God-facing motive is compared while retaining Peter's different immediate setting of household slaves and masters.

Both connect payment of tribute or taxes with obligation under God. Romans describes the authorities as God's ministers; Jesus answers the tribute question by distinguishing rendering Caesar's things and God's things.

Both list owed honor and fear in a context that includes public authority. Peter specifically assigns fear to God and honor to the king; Romans lists the respective dues without naming each recipient.
Both make love of another or neighbor the fulfillment of law. Galatians explicitly cites the neighbor-love saying; Romans introduces that principle through the continuing obligation to love.

Paul's four prohibitions correspond to adultery, murder, theft and coveting in the Decalogue. The pinned Greek-order Exodus places theft before murder and includes false witness in this span; Romans does not reproduce that intervening command.
Romans quotes the command to love one's neighbor as oneself as the summary of the prohibitions. Leviticus gives that command alongside the prohibition of vengeance and continued anger.

Romans says love does no evil to the neighbor. Corinthians describes love as not seeking its own interests, not keeping account of wrong and not rejoicing in unrighteousness; it expands love's conduct without repeating the law-fulfillment formulation.

Both join the approaching day with ethical wakefulness and salvation. Thessalonians develops light, day, vigilance and the hope of salvation; it does not repeat Romans's comparison with the time when believers first believed.

Both contrast day and light with night and darkness and use putting-on imagery for readiness. Romans names weapons of light; Thessalonians specifies a breastplate of faith and love and a helmet of salvation's hope.

The vice lists overlap specifically in licentiousness, strife, jealousy, drunkenness and revelries, alongside sexual wrongdoing. Romans contrasts this conduct with honorable daytime living; Galatians calls its catalogue works of the flesh.
Both use the distinctive image of putting on Christ. Galatians relates it to baptism into Christ; Romans uses it as an exhortation and adds the rejection of provision for fleshly desires.

The later instruction repeats welcoming one another and grounds it in Christ's welcome. It develops the present instruction to welcome the person weak in faith without turning reception into disputes over opinions.

Both discuss weakness in connection with eating or abstaining. Romans names vegetables and weak faith; Corinthians names idol-associated food and a weak conscience. This does not identify the groups or supply an unstated reason for Roman abstinence.
Both reject judging people over eating. Romans addresses reciprocal contempt and judgment between eaters and abstainers whom God welcomes; Colossians also includes drinking and calendar observances.

Both challenge judging a brother or neighbor by asking who the human judge is in relation to the Lord's authority. Romans uses another master's household slave and the Lord's ability to make him stand; James names the one Lawgiver and Judge.

Both discuss religious distinctions involving days. Romans contrasts regarding one day and regarding all alike and requires personal conviction; Colossians warns against judgment over festival, new moon or Sabbaths and calls them a shadow.

Both connect eating with thanksgiving and a God-directed purpose. Romans also includes abstaining and regarding a day for the Lord; Corinthians speaks of thankful participation and doing eating, drinking and all else for God's glory.

Romans denies that believers live for themselves. Corinthians similarly says those who live should no longer live for themselves but for the One who died and was raised; Romans additionally includes dying in its statement.

Romans says believers belong to the Lord whether living or dying. Corinthians says they are not their own because they were bought at a price and therefore should glorify God in the body; the common point is belonging rather than self-ownership.

Romans connects Christ's dying and living with His lordship over dead and living. Peter's speech describes God raising Jesus and appointing Him judge of living and dead. The titles Lord and judge and the two formulations remain distinct.

Both say that all will face the judgment seat. The pinned Romans text calls it God's judgment seat; Corinthians calls it Christ's and specifies receiving what is due for bodily deeds. The names are preserved rather than normalized.

The written saying about every knee bending and every tongue confessing to God is found in Isaiah's divine oath. Romans introduces it with the Lord's living oath formula rather than reproducing Isaiah's opening 'By Myself I swear'.

Both speak of giving an account before divine judgment. Romans applies the statement to each of us before God; Peter's immediate subjects are people slandering believers, who must answer to the One judging living and dead.

Both warn against placing a stumbling block before another believer in the setting of food choices. Corinthians specifically warns that one's authority may become a stumbling block to the weak; Romans redirects judgment toward avoiding such harm.

Romans distinguishes food's uncleanness from the person's reckoning it unclean. Corinthians describes a weak conscience defiled while eating food as idol-associated. Both consider the eater's religious understanding, without importing Corinthians's stated idol background into Romans.

Both warn that a brother for whom Christ died can be destroyed through another believer's use of food or knowledge. Corinthians further calls striking the weak conscience a sin against Christ; Romans contrasts the harmful choice with walking in love.

Both discuss being spoken against in the food-and-conscience setting. Romans warns against letting one's good be spoken of as evil; Corinthians asks why freedom is judged by another conscience and thankful participation is slandered.

Both associate joy and peace with the Spirit. Romans describes the kingdom through righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit rather than eating and drinking; Galatians includes joy and peace in the fruit of the Spirit.

Both coordinate conduct before God and people: serving Christ in the stated way is pleasing to God and approved by people, while the collection administrators take care for what is honorable before both Lord and people. The immediate activities differ.

Both prioritize building others up in the context of food liberty. Corinthians distinguishes permission from what builds up and commands seeking the other's good; Romans urges pursuit of peace and mutual building.

Romans warns against tearing down God's work for food and distinguishes cleanness from eating with stumbling. Corinthians likewise describes food-related freedom and knowledge that can become a stumbling block and destroy a weak brother.

Both favor foregoing food rather than causing a brother to stumble. Corinthians states Paul's resolve never to eat meat if food causes that harm; Romans explicitly also names wine and anything else that makes the brother stumble.

The blessing of not judging oneself in what one approves is followed by the opposite case: a doubting eater is condemned because the eating is not from faith. This is an internal contrast between stated convictions and outcomes in the same food discussion.

Both make faith necessary for conduct acceptable to God. Romans's immediate example is a doubting eater; Hebrews speaks of approaching God in belief that He exists and rewards seekers. The comparison preserves these different applications of faith.
